conversion.wien_note: Frequency of the B_ν maximum is ≈ 58.8 GHz × T/K (CITED, Planck). A 0.1–10 K thermal spectrum is roughly 10 GHz–1 THz, with the 1 K peak at 59 GHz and the 4 K peak at 235 GHz.

scatter_only_ceiling.note: DERIVED: Im χ = 0, so only blackbody scattering (depends on Re χ, not loss) plus air and GGN. This is the hard T_env ceiling for a perfect crystal.

cases.label: Stage 12 assumption
cases.note: ASSUMED in Stage 12, not a measurement. Equivalent tanδ ≈ 0.035 at ε′=5.7, in the range of heavily defective / graphitic carbon rather than diamond.
cases.source: Stage 12, chosen as a conservative 10× reduction from Romero-Isart silica Im χ = 0.1

cases.label: Fused silica (Romero-Isart 2011)
cases.band: thermal / IR, as used for silica nanospheres
cases.note: CITED: Romero-Isart, Phys. Rev. A 84, 052121 (2011), Table III, ε_bb = 2.1 + i 0.57, which gives Im[(ε-1)/(ε+2)] = 0.1. This is silica, not diamond. Included only as the number QGEM-adjacent optomechanics inherited.

cases.label: Best optical-grade poly-CVD (window)
cases.band: 170 GHz, 300 K (record); window-grade material is similar or slightly better at 70–100 K
cases.note: CITED Garin / Parshin / Derkach et al.: record tanδ ≈ 4.5×10^{-6} at 170 GHz, 300 K, still ~10× above the theoretical phonon floor. Typical optical-grade “Diamond Materials” poly-CVD is specified at tanδ ≈ 10^{-5} in the 100–200 GHz band (CITED Mazzocchi et al. 2026, quoting the manufacturer).
cases.source: Garin et al., NASA/CR and Diamond Relat. Mater. (2003–2005); Mazzocchi et al., arXiv:2512.03780 (2026)

cases.label: Typical window-grade CVD
cases.band: 100–200 GHz, 300 K (and the usual gyrotron-window specification)
cases.note: CITED typical specification for optical-grade polycrystalline CVD used as gyrotron windows. JJAP 2025 reports 2×10^{-6}–3.5×10^{-5} over 10–330 GHz on a 2-inch poly wafer, decreasing with frequency in the 220–330 GHz band. Single-crystal CVD wafers: tanδ ≤ 2×10^{-5} at 145–170 GHz (Yamada et al., Diamond Relat. Mater. 58, 1 (2015)).
cases.source: Diamond Materials spec as quoted by Mazzocchi arXiv:2512.03780; Dang et al. JJAP (2025); Yamada et al. DRM 2015

cases.label: Poly-CVD at 22 GHz, 35–100 K (Millar)
cases.band: 22.3 GHz, 35–100 K (this sample); 22 GHz sits near the 0.4 K Wien peak and is relevant to 1 K tails
cases.note: CITED Millar, le Floch, Tobar et al., arXiv:1302.4149 (Diamond Materials poly-CVD disk). Fits: tanδ(T)=7.950×10^{-4} T^{0.045} for T<100 K (almost flat; ≈ 9.3×10^{-4} at 35 K) and 2.137×10^{-4} T^{0.329} for T>100 K. This sample is much lossier at 22 GHz than window-grade material at 170 GHz, consistent with a conductivity / defect 1/f tail. VDK 2020 cites this group (Le Floch / Hartnett / Tobar) when treating ε as “real” at O(1) K — that is fair for Re(ε)≈5.67, but Im χ is not zero.
cases.source: Millar et al. arXiv:1302.4149; van de Kamp et al. PRA 102, 062807 (2020) ref. [53]

cases.label: Same poly-CVD at 0.67–1 THz, 300 K
cases.note: CITED Millar et al.: ε* = 5.661 (1 − j 6.3×10^{-5}) around 1 THz. Loss decreases with frequency relative to their 22 GHz data. Room-temperature THz data are a useful upper envelope for 10 K thermal photons, but the cryogenic 22 GHz number is more conservative near 1 K.

cases.label: Single-crystal CVD, sub-K microwave
cases.note: CITED Mazzocchi et al., arXiv:2512.03780 (2026), Table I: lowest measured total tanδ ≈ 2.04×10^{-6} (IrSCD), 5.94×10^{-6} (HPHT-seeded CVD clone); optical-grade poly-CVD 1.04×10^{-5}. Nitrogen-related TLS floors tanδ_TLS^0 ≈ 7×10^{-6}–2.4×10^{-5}. TLS loss typically *falls* from millikelvin to a few kelvin as two-level systems saturate, so these are conservative for a 1–10 K thermal-photon budget if other channels do not take over. A tiled-clone joint reached tanδ = 1.44×10^{-4} from boundary scattering, a warning that defects dominate when they are present.
cases.source: Mazzocchi, Yamada, Scherer et al., arXiv:2512.03780 (24 Aug 2026 / dated in preprint)

cases.label: Nanodiamond with surface sp² (dirty)
cases.band: microwave 2.5–9 GHz (powders); used as a conservative effective tanδ for a micron particle with a graphitic / disordered shell
cases.note: CITED Cuenca et al., ACS Omega 3, 2183 (2018): microwave tanδ of sub-micron diamond powders tracks surface sp²; 5% sp² is detectable; they extrapolate tanδ ≈ 0.016 at 100% sp² (2.5 GHz). ASSUMED effective tanδ = 10^{-2} for a “dirty” NV nanodiamond (HPHT-crushed, residual graphitic shell). A DERIVED core-shell check: a 2 nm shell with order-unity effective loss on a 0.73 μm radius core gives a volume fraction 3 ΔR/R ≈ 0.8% and an effective tanδ of the same order (10^{-3}–10^{-2}) if the shell is graphitic. Detonation ND and uncleaned commercial NV powder can be in this range or worse. THz-TDS on NCD films (e.g. ACS Appl. Electron. Mater. 2020) attributes 0.1–3 THz absorption fingerprints to sp² / grain-boundary phases.
cases.source: Cuenca et al., ACS Omega 3, 2183 (2018); core-shell estimate DERIVED; THz-TDS qualitative from Liu et al., ACS AEM (2020)

cases.label: Cleaner milled CVD nanodiamond
cases.band: effective, microwave-to-THz; ASSUMED mid-range between window-grade bulk and dirty-surface powder
cases.note: ASSUMED 10^{-3}, not a direct THz measurement on a single 0.7 μm sphere. Motivated by: (i) Millar’s cryogenic 22 GHz poly-CVD already sits here even without a surface shell; (ii) milled high-purity CVD nanodiamonds show far less near-IR absorption / laser heating than commercial HPHT NV powder (Frangeskou et al., NJP 20, 043016 (2018), arXiv:1608.04724); (iii) a thinner or less graphitic shell (0.5–1 nm, moderate tanδ) gives a similar effective number. This is the cautious “realistic NV particle” case, not a claim of a measured 10^{-3}.
cases.source: Scale set by Millar 2013 + Cuenca 2018 + Frangeskou 2018; the 10^{-3} value itself is ASSUMED

qgem_assumptions.romero_isart_2011: Silica, not diamond: ε_bb=2.1+i0.57, Im[(ε-1)/(ε+2)]=0.1. CITED PRA 84, 052121 Table III. The Stage 12 default Im χ=0.01 was a 10× “diamond is cleaner than silica” guess, not a measurement.
qgem_assumptions.yin_2013: Yin et al., Phys. Rev. A 88, 033614 (2013), arXiv:1305.1701, state that the THz emission rate of diamond is “smaller by about two orders of magnitude” than the silica sphere of Romero-Isart, implying Im χ ~ 10^{-3} for diamond at (room-temperature) THz. They do not cite a tanδ measurement. 10^{-3} is 300× larger than window-grade mm-wave Im χ, and is closer to our dirty-nanodiamond / Millar-22 GHz cases.
qgem_assumptions.vdk_2020: van de Kamp et al., PRA 102, 062807, treat ε as real and T-independent at T~O(1) K, citing Ibarra et al. (Diamond Relat. Mater. 1997) and Le Floch / Hartnett / Tobar (the Millar 2013 data set). They note that for diamond, phonon excitations are negligible below T_int < 4 K (citing Bose 2017). They never quote Im[(ε-1)/(ε+2)]. They say air dominates and T_int can be raised to a few kelvin “without interfering with the results significantly.” That conclusion holds for window-grade Im χ; it is tight for Im χ=0.01 and for dirty nanodiamond.
qgem_assumptions.schut_2024: Schut et al., PRR 6, 013199, cite blackbody and air as a decoherence package and take γ ~ 10^{-2} Hz at ~1 K from earlier papers. No independent Im χ.
qgem_assumptions.bose_2017: Bose et al. PRL 2017 mention internal cooling / Tint and diamond phonons, without a loss-tangent number.

heating.magnetic_trap: The Stage 12 cheap point is magnetically trapped (Schut 2024 layout). There is no 1064 nm optical-trap beam during the hold, which removes the dominant heating channel of levitated-optomechanics experiments.
heating.nv_laser: CITED Frangeskou et al., New J. Phys. 20, 043016 (2018), arXiv:1608.04724: commercial HPHT NV nanodiamonds in an optical dipole trap have been reported above 800 K at modest vacuum (absorption by nitrogen and amorphous/graphitic defects). Milled high-purity CVD nanodiamonds showed no measurable laser-power-dependent heating up to ~300 mW at 3–4 mbar. Any green/IR NV initialization or readout laser left on during the 2.5 s hold, in 10^{-15} Pa, would likely raise T_int far above the 15–20 K emission ceiling. Lasers must be off (or used only at the start/end, with time to cool) for the budget below to apply.
heating.radiative_cooling: At 1–4 K the radiative coupling of a 0.73 μm sphere is weak, especially if Im χ is window-grade (10^{-6}). The DERIVED order-of-magnitude radiative time constant τ ~ C_V T / P_em is seconds to many hours, depending on Im χ and T (see cases). Residual gas conduction is negligible at 2.4×10^{-15} Pa. So T_int is set by whatever it was after loading / last laser pulse, not by T_env, unless a long wait or an active cooling step is built in. Internal temperature is the binding thermal variable.

verdict_one_liner: Window-grade diamond is comfortable at a 4 K cryostat and only dies of blackbody (mostly scattering) near 12–14 K; the Stage 12 “dead at 5 K” cliff was the Im χ=0.01 assumption. Dirty nanodiamond surfaces bring the cliff back to ~4–6 K. Internal temperature, not T_env, is binding if any laser is used in vacuum.
